overview: KeepRange is a combat keep-distance assist (aliased S Tap) that rewrites the client's movement input instead of touching packets. A MoveInputEvent listener polls TargetComponent.getTarget(10) and, when the target is closer than the Range setting (0 to 6, default 3, stepped 0.1, shrunk by 0.2 while ticksSinceAttack is within 7), steers the forward and strafe input onto the bearing directly away from the target: the away angle is the wrapped target yaw plus 180 degrees, and the module scores the eight input combinations (forward and strafe each in -1, 0, 1) by wrapped difference, keeping the closest one. Stop mode zeroes whichever input component opposes the away direction; BackWards mode overwrites both components with the winning away combination. The rewrite feeds the vanilla input pipeline, so the resulting motion rides the ordinary C03 stream as a stop or a backward walk, and the C02 attack stream that the module exists to service comes from the paired combat module.

sections.p: The MoveInputEvent handler computes the away bearing from RotationUtil.calculate(target).getX() plus 180 degrees wrapped into -180..180, then brute-forces the eight forward/strafe combinations through MoveUtil.direction(rotationYaw, predictedForward, predictedStrafe) and keeps the combination whose direction is closest to the away bearing by MathUtil.wrappedDifference. In Stop mode, if the winning combination's forward component is the negation of the current forward input, forward is zeroed, and the same for strafe; in BackWards mode both components are replaced outright. The switch between the two modes is a SubMode pair, with Stop as the default.

Three gates decide whether the steering runs. The combo gate counts target.hurtTime ticks into a row counter: row increments while the target is hurt, resets when the local player is hurt, and the steering only starts once row exceeds Combo To Start times 8 (default 16 hurt ticks at the default combo of 2). The edge gate scans the block column with PlayerUtil.blockRelativeToPlayer over x and z in the Edge Range square (default 5) and y from -5 to 0, and when any column is entirely air the player is marked at an edge; with Disable Near Edge (default on) the steering shuts off there. The third gate is the range shrink: within 7 ticks after an attack the effective range drops by 0.2, so the module backs off sooner right after swinging. The range comparison itself uses PlayerUtil.calculatePerfectRangeToEntity against range minus 0.05.

No packet is sent, cancelled or rewritten. The steering changes the move input that the client's movement code consumes, so the wire only shows the outcome: a decelerating or backward-walking player whose positions always stay inside the physics envelope. Backward walking at full speed is a normal vanilla motion (negative forward input), and an instant stop is indistinguishable from a released key. The module is invisible to server-side checks; the countering set below documents the boundaries and why each stays silent.

files.label: KeepRange.java
files.explanation: The complete module. The MoveInputEvent listener holds the entire steering logic: the away-bearing computation, the eight-combination direction search, and the Stop/BackWards rewrite. The GameEvent listener maintains the edge flag by scanning the block column around the player, and the row counter implements the combo gate from target.hurtTime ticks. The module imports TargetComponent, MoveUtil, RotationUtil and PlayerUtil but emits no packets: its output is the modified forward and strafe input consumed by the client's movement pipeline.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (movement physics envelope)
countering.explanation: SurvivalFly rebuilds the physics envelope from the world and only punishes motion that exceeds it: horizontal allowance from prepareSpeedEstimation, vertical from vDistRel, violation (max(hDistanceAboveLimit, 0) plus max(yDistanceAboveLimit, 0)) times 100 with a set-back to the stored location. The KeepRange steering produces exactly the motions the envelope was built to allow: a stop (zero horizontal delta) and a backward walk at walking speed, both within the friction-derived allowance. An instant stop is the same profile as a released key or a wall collision, which the model tolerates because it bounds acceleration upward rather than deceleration. The check is an honest boundary: it would only fire if the steering ever produced motion outside the envelope, which the input-level rewrite cannot do.

countering.label: Speed (horizontal accumulator)
countering.explanation: Arc v2's Speed check scores each move against the walking expectation: baseMove 0.2873 times the speed-potion multiplier, stage allowances, pending velocity, with an instant cancel above 8 blocks in a single move. The BackWards mode's override produces backward movement at walking speed, and the check's expected model is direction-agnostic: a negative forward input yields the same expected magnitude as a positive one, so the reversal is scored as an ordinary walk. The Stop mode's zero-delta moves score below the expectation and accumulate nothing. Both outputs stay inside the model, and the module is invisible to the check by construction.

countering.label: Speed (prev-speed progression)
countering.explanation: Hawk Speed predicts the next speed from the previous one: expected equals friction times lastSpeed times multipliers plus maxForce plus epsilon, and only moves faster than expected accumulate discrepancy toward the 0.1 threshold. The module's direction reversal looks like a legit input flip: the vanilla move-flying pipeline accumulates the new input onto the existing motion, so the forward-to-backward transition decays through friction exactly as it would for a player who flicked the key, and the predicted progression tracks it. The Stop mode's deceleration is likewise within the model, which never punishes speed drops (walls and released keys produce the same profile). The check is one-directional by design, and the input rewrite stays on the legitimate side of it.

countering.label: Reach (attack distance)
countering.explanation: NCP fight Reach measures the attack distance against the server's current victim position, with a survival distance limit of 4.02 in this tree (DefaultConfig line 366) and a reachMod reduce band that silently cancels repeat hits below the limit. The module's entire purpose is to keep the attack stream inside that window: it backs the player off when the target gets closer than the Range setting, so the C02 packets the paired combat module sends land at a controlled distance. Reach sees a compliant, in-range stream and never fires, which is the module succeeding at its own design goal rather than a detection. The honest framing is that Reach bounds the attack stream the module services, not the module itself, and the module would be invisible even if the attacks were absent.
